content:
Hi everyone! I wanted to share a project I have been working on for the past couple of weeks: ChessProver.

My goal is to build a two-player chess engine in Lean, together with a rich theory for proving statements about chess, especially endgames.

Chess endgames are famously subtle. In pawn endgames, even whose turn it is can completely change the result. When you first learn about chess endgames, you are usually taught how to corner the king with a queen or rook, alongside ideas such as the ladder mate, opposition, and shouldering the opposing king. I thought it would be interesting to formalize some of this theory in Lean.

With help from Codex, I built the underlying chess player. It has a simple CLI and implements the standard rules, including castling, promotion, and en passant. On top of the engine, I have begun developing a theory layer where chess statements can be expressed and proved.

As a proof of concept, I asked: what is the simplest endgame to formalize? King+Rook vs King? King+Queen vs King? No, just King vs King :)

I have now proved that in a legal King vs King endgame, neither side can checkmate the other.
I plan to continue with King + Queen vs King. King + pawn vs King will be the next major milestone.

Anyway, I just wanted to share this project with the community.

The README explains how the engine and theory are structured.
Project: https://github.com/parabamoghv/ChessProver

Suggestions, comments, and formalization ideas are very welcome!
See also https://github.com/dwrensha/Chess.lean

One way to proceed here, since endgame rules are discovered by table base (EGTB) software, would be to prove the correctness of this software via Lean and recompute the table bases. This would catch at least all (up to) 6 piece endgames.
This topic was moved here from #general > ChessProver: formalizing chess and endgames in Lean by Michael Rothgang.

I would not be as optimistic as 6 piece endgames, I think the first goal should just be something, e.g. 3 piece endgames (already this is subtle, e.g. K+R v K you need a proof that mate can be achieved in 99.9% of cases, K+B v K you need a proof that it cannot, and K+P v K is delicate). Sounds like 2 piece endgames have already been done so 3 pieces is the next natural challenge. It would be cool to have a Lean-powered opponent which can play K+P v K perfectly. This sounds like a great test case.

I remember GNUchess implemented perfect evaluation of KPK (the original paper by ? had 50-100 lines of BASIC like IF ... THEN ... ELSE, which I translated to C for them) but they abandoned it because in a game you need an increasing evaluation to make progress. Current EGTB all have that.

Note also, there is no way to find simple rules for endgames. KPK already has dozens, and I used early ML (C4.5) to find rules for KPKP but found none that were better than just using a tablebase.

There are probably interesting things to prove about n×nn\times nn×n (or m×nm\times nm×n) boards, not just 8×88\times88×8. See e.g. a paper on KBNK discussing (not proving optimal) asymptotics for that endgame on an n×nn\times nn×n board. (But certainly KQK or KRK must be easier to prove things about there than KBNK.)

Ralf Stephan said:

One way to proceed here, since endgame rules are discovered by table base (EGTB) software, would be to prove the correctness of this software via Lean and recompute the table bases.

It shouldn't be necessary to prove the correctness of the software or recompute the tablebases, should it? Once the tablebases are computed, verifying that they are correct is a lot easier than computing them in the first place. But maybe Lean is not well equipped to deal with such large files?

There are a couple of subtle points about tablebases to be careful about, if we want truly rigorous proofs. An obvious one is the fifty-move rule. A second subtlety is that a complete description of the current state of a chess game includes not just the board position, but a little bit of "historical" information. Suppose we have the White king on e1, a White rook on a1, a Black rook on c2, the Black king on d8, and it's White to move. The tablebases will tell you that this is a draw, but if White has not yet moved either the king or the rook and therefore still has the right to castle, then castling (with check) wins the rook and the game. This "historical" aspect of chess means that so-called "retrograde analysis" can come into play. For example, in the position we just described, for White to be able to castle, Black's last move must have been a capture, and the capture could not have been capturing a White pawn with ...Rxc2.

Finally, there are some very obscure rules that probably don't matter even for a Lean proof. Look up "75 move rule" and "fivefold repetition" and "dead reckoning" (in the context of chess, of course) if you're curious.

The endgame table base is just a mammoth database. I used it to check some pawn endgames. I can also see that in larger endgames, there is no way to avoid it. As @Kevin Buzzard suggested, my next goal is a 3-piece endgame, specifically KQvK. The idea for formalization, in essence, is to show that the attacking player can always put the defending king in a smaller cage. When the cage is small enough (but not too small), you can deliver a mate.

I agree with @Ralf Stephan that the definition of classification for KPvK to win or draw will make many if... else ... then. When the time comes to actually write this function, I can see myself ducking out and importing egdb of KPvK. Having said that, my initial focus is on formalization of endgame chess tactics. For example, the main subgoal in KPvK is to create a "red carpet" for a pawn (king on the 7 th rank adjacent to the pawn file) so that the pawn walks the red carpet to become a queen. Once I have enough of these tactics, it would be easier to plug those in when required.

Also, @Ralf Stephan, I couldn't find the paper you were talking about. If you don't mind, could you help me locate it? It would be cool to see what kind of if...else they used.

I think @Timothy Chow makes some good points about the EGTB. I don't know if EGTB enforces 50 moves or 3-fold repetition. There are some winning endgames that you don't enforce the 50-move rule on that are otherwise draws. IMO, 3-fold repetition and 50-move rules are arbitrary, and for chess theory they can be ignored.

My implementation of chess has two layers: a core chess engine that does not enforce these rules and a chess player (CLI) on top of that that enforces these rules. As far as proofs go, they concern the core engine. If you notice, in the KK endgame, I state that no side can checkmate and not that it is a drawn game.

Similarly, insufficient material could be subsumed by the proposition that player(s) cannot enforce a checkmate.

@Joseph Myers, that is a cool paper you shared. Endgames on arbitrarily large boards. If I had to guess which winning endgame on the usual board is not winning on arbitrarily large boards, I would have said KBNvK. Apparently that is not the case.

I just checked EGTB; KNNNvK is winning on the usual board. Maybe that's a candidate?

The converse seems true. If an endgame is winning on arbitrarily large boards, it should be winning on the usual board. Interesting nonetheless.
The 75 move rule was removed a long time ago; it's not in the current laws of chess. (I do have a 1989 printed edition that includes it.)

Tablebases may be calculated for DTM (depth to mate) or DTC (depth to conversion, i.e. capture, promotion or mate) or DTZ (depth to move that zeroes the 50-move-rule count, i.e. conversion or pawn move) or DTR (minimum nnn in place of 50 in the 50-move rule for which it's possible to win). All of DTM, DTC and DTZ are implicitly assuming you don't have a 50-move rule.
Slight tangent, but it would be nice to have an efficient bitboard move generator that is proved equivalent to a "naive" implementation that someone could more easily verify correct.

Amogh said:

Also, Ralf Stephan, I couldn't find the paper you were talking about. If you don't mind, could you help me locate it? It would be cool to see what kind of if...else they used.

I couldn't find it either, sorry. But this one has flow diagrams and Fortran code: Piasetski, Leon. An evaluation function for simple King and Pawn endings. McGill University (Canada), 1977. PDF: https://mcgill.scholaris.ca/bitstreams/cb87f0fb-e682-41ba-a647-f205dd6c108f/download

Most tablebases do not take into account the 50-move rule, except in the sense that Joseph Myers said, of tracking DTZ. If you're uncertain about a particular tablebase, you could for example put in a KBBvKN position that requires more than 50 moves to win, and see what it says. I'm sure that tablebases don't track threefold repetition either; first of all, it can never be relevant if we assume that all preceding play was perfect, and second, a fully rigorous implementation would require tracking every previously occurring position that could still occur in the future, which would be total insanity.

@Joseph Myers I think that your link is not to the current Laws of Chess. Try this link instead. One way to tell if you're viewing the 2023 version is that it uses "he/she".
Interesting, thanks (I was taking the first Google hit I found, and thinking of an older 75-move rule from when the 50-move rule had variations for a few specific endgames).

A long time ago I tried to prove that given a board with (only) 8 white pawns on the first rank, and 8 black pawns on the last rank, you can't exchange them (ignoring promotion). Didn't get there. :-) There might be an ancient conversation on this Zulip.

Hi! Progress has slowed since the semester started, but I can share the current direction.

I shifted the focus toward a general formalization of turn-based games and endgames. In particular, I am working on competitive and cooperative games, formalizing which results a player or players can force. I am also developing a guided tree-search tactic: on friendly turns the prover (human or AI) supplies a move, while on opponent turns it expands the resulting legal-move goals. That core direction is in place; I now want to realize chess within this formulation. I will write another post once that is further along.

Please feel free to use and cite the development. I thought I had already added a licence, but I will make sure to add one.

Proof-number search is a very cool idea; thank you for mentioning it. I have a feeling that this might be relevant for me, but I am sure there is much more for me to learn.

Probably for normal speed search one would need to port parts of, for example, Stockfish. So, yes, +1 to this.
